Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 44, verses 11–18:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿Covering the people. This is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed, we are believers.﴾ ﴿How can they have the reminder, when a clear Messenger has already come to them?﴾ ﴿Then they turned away from him and said, "A taught one, a madman."﴾ ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little; indeed, you will return [to disbelief].﴾ ﴿On the Day We seize with the greatest seizing; indeed, We will take retribution.﴾ ﴿And We had already tested before them the people of Pharaoh, and there came to them a noble Messenger,﴾ ﴿[saying], "Deliver to me the servants of Allah. Indeed, I am a trustworthy Messenger to you."﴾

"Yaghsha" (يَغْشى): its meaning is "covers." His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿This is a painful punishment﴾, may be a report from Allah, Exalted is He, as if He is marveling at it, similar to His saying when He described the story of the sacrifice: ﴿Indeed, this is the clear trial﴾ [al-Saffat: 106]. It may also be that ﴿This is a painful punishment﴾ is the words of the people, as if the sense is: they say, "This is a painful punishment." The context supports this interpretation, as He, Exalted is He, relates of them that they say: ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed, we are believers.﴾ Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, knew that their saying in the state of hardship, ﴿indeed, we are believers﴾, was not from them in truth. So He indicated this by His saying: ﴿How can they have the reminder?﴾, meaning: from where can they have the means to be reminded, when they have cast the reminder behind their backs, since there has come to them a clear Messenger, who is Muhammad (ﷺ), and they disbelieved in him? "Then they turned away from him" means they turned away. They said that he was taught this speech that he recites and that he was a madman. Allah's statement that He will remove the punishment from them a little is a report about the establishment of the proof against them and an exaggeration in granting them respite. Then Allah, Exalted is He, reported that they would return to disbelief. Qatadah said that this is a warning of the return in the Hereafter. Then Allah, Exalted is He, reported that He would take retribution from them, because of all this (p-573), on the Day of the Seizing. He placed the Day first and mentioned it before that which operates upon it, to emphasize it and to frighten them with it. The word that governs it is "muntaqimun" (مُنْتَقِمُونَ). The Basran grammarians criticized this, on the grounds that it is the predicate of "inna" (إنَّ), and they considered it unlikely that the predicate of "inna" should govern what precedes it. They said the governing element is a hidden verb indicated by "munta-qimun" (مُنْتَقِمُونَ).

People differed concerning the Day of the Great Seizing. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah and Qatadah said it is the Day of Resurrection. 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas also (in another report), Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Mujahid said it is the Day of Badr. The majority of readers recited "nabtishu" (نَبْطِشُ) with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the ta'. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read it with a damma on the ta'. As for "the noble Messenger," Qatadah said he is Musa, peace be upon him. As for the springs, it is possible that he meant the canals issuing from the Nile, and he likened them to springs; it is also possible that there were springs there which dried up, as happens in many regions of the earth. Likewise al-Yamani read it throughout the Qur'an except in Maryam (p-577) ﴿khayrun maqāman﴾ [Maryam: 73]. So the meaning is: how many good places, noble in their worth and benefit, they left behind. On the ḍamma of the mīm in "muqām", Qatada said: it means the fine dwellings and other places. The view that these are pulpits is very fine indeed.

Afflictions, pains and calamities may be blessings, yet they are not called naʿmah with a fatḥa. Abū Rajāʾ read ﴿"wa-niʿmatan"﴾ in the accusative. The majority of people read ﴿"fākihīn"﴾ in the sense of "delighting". Al-fākih is one whose soul is joyful; or it may mean "possessors of fruit", like laabin and tamir. Abū Rajāʾ, al-Hasan (in a variant from him) and Ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ read ﴿"fakihīn"﴾, and its meaning is close to the first; but fakih is often used of one who is light-hearted and mocking, so it is as if here it says: they were in this blessing, light-heartedly disregarding its thanks and not knowing its due right.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Thus. And We made it an inheritance﴾ means: the matter is thus, and He called it inheritance because the belongings of people passed to other people after the death of the first ones, and this is the real meaning of inheritance in the language; the Sharia linked it to kinship and other causes of inheritance. And "the others" refers to the rule over Egypt after the Copts. Qatada said: the other people are the Children of Israel; but this is weak, because it is not reported in the histories that the Children of Israel returned to Egypt at any time in that era, nor did they ever rule it, unless Qatada means that they inherited its kind in the lands of Syria. Al-Tha'labi related from al-Hasan that the Children of Israel returned to Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 44, verse 19–28:

﴿And do not exalt yourselves against Allah. Indeed, I bring you a clear authority.﴾ ﴿And indeed, I seek refuge in my Lord and your Lord, lest you stone me.﴾ ﴿And if you do not believe me, then leave me alone.﴾ ﴿So he called upon his Lord, "Indeed, these are a criminal people."﴾ ﴿So set out with My servants by night; indeed, you will be pursued.﴾ ﴿And leave the sea parted; indeed, they are an army to be drowned.﴾ ﴿How many gardens and springs they left behind,﴾ ﴿and crops and a noble station,﴾ ﴿and luxury in which they had been delighting.﴾ ﴿Thus. And We made it an inheritance for another people.﴾

The meaning: His message and his saying were: "Deliver [the believers to me] and do not exalt yourselves," and he expressed by "exaltation" (ʿulūw) the insolent defiance and arrogance against Allah, the Exalted, against His law, and against His Messenger. The majority (al-Jumhūr) read ﴿"Innī ātīkum"﴾ with a kasra on the alif of "innī", as a emphatic declarative statement. And al-sulṭān (authority) means the proof, so it is as if he said: "Do not disbelieve, for the evidence leading to faith is clear." A group read "Annī ātīkum" with a fatḥa on the alif. "An" is in the place of a naṣb (accusative), with the meaning: "Do not disbelieve on account of my bringing you a clear authority." So the intent of the speech is rebuke, as when you say to a person: "Do not be angry, for the truth has been told to you."

And his saying: ﴿And indeed I seek refuge﴾ [the verse] is a statement that Musa, peace be upon him, made because of a fear that befell him from Pharaoh and his chieftains. "ʿUdtu" means: I sought protection and made myself inviolable. Al-Aʿraj and Abū ʿAmr assimilated the dhāl into the tāʾ. People differed regarding his saying: ﴿"an tarjumūn"﴾. Qatada and others said: he meant stoning with stones, leading to death. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Abū Ṣāliḥ said: he meant stoning with words, such as insult, opposition and the like. The first is more apparent, because he sought refuge from it, whereas he did not seek refuge from the second, rather it was said about him, peace be upon him, and in his favour. His saying: ﴿tuʾminū lī﴾ means: "you believe in me" [i.e., lī is equivalent to bī], and the meaning is: "you accept as true." His saying: ﴿"fa-ʿtazilūn"﴾ is an explicit disengagement. Qatada said: he meant "leave my path."

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿So he called upon his Lord﴾ has before it something omitted from the speech, its estimate being: so they did not refrain from him, rather they attacked him, and transgressed against him and against his call; so he called upon his Lord. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and ʿIsa read ﴿"inna hāʾulāʾ"﴾ with a kasra on the alif of "inna", in the sense of "he said: indeed". The majority of people, and al-Hasan also, read ﴿"anna hāʾulāʾ"﴾ with a fatḥa on the alif. Both readings are good. He judged them with criminality that implies disbelief, when he despaired of them. Here too something is omitted from the speech, its estimate being: Allah, the Exalted, said to him: "So set out with My servants," and this is the command that Allah, the Exalted, sent down to Musa, peace be upon him, to leave the land of Egypt with the Children of Israel. Its explanation and narrative have already been mentioned in Surat al-Anbiya' and elsewhere. The majority of people read ﴿"fasri"﴾ with a connected alif, while al-Hasan, ʿIsa, and what is narrated from Abū ʿAmr read ﴿"fa-asri"﴾ with a cut alif. (p-575) Allah informed him that they will be pursued, that is, Pharaoh and his soldiers will pursue them.

The exegetes differed regarding His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And leave the sea parted﴾: when did He, glory be to Him and exalted, say it to Musa, peace be upon him? One group said: it is a connected statement, meaning: "you will be pursued, and leave the sea, when it has split for you, parted." Qatada and others said: he, peace be upon him, was addressed with it after he had crossed the sea and feared that Pharaoh and his people would enter behind him, and would come out by the routes through which the Children of Israel had come out; so Musa, peace be upon him, intended to strike the sea, perhaps it would close up and return to its state. So it was said to him at that moment: ﴿And leave the sea parted﴾.

The wording of the exegetes differed concerning the interpretation of ar-rahw. Mujahid and ʿIkrima said: its meaning is "dry", from His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Strike for them a dry path through the sea﴾ [Ṭāhā: 77]. Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim said: its meaning is "soft and gentle". ʿIkrima also said: "bare". Ibn Zayd said: "easy". Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: its meaning is "still", i.e., as it was when it was crossed. This last view is the one that the language supports, for the ar-rāhī life is one of ease, tranquillity and calm; this was related by al-Mubarrad and others. Ar-rahw in the language has this meaning, and from it is the saying of ʿUmayr ibn Shuyaym al-Qaṭāmī:

> They walk at ease; neither the hinder parts failing [their front] nor the chests relying upon the hinder parts.

Its meaning is: they walk with deliberation, stillness and leisureliness. And from it is the saying of another:

> ............................ or a nation went out at ease to a festival.

That is: they went out in stillness and leisureliness. So it was said to Musa, peace be upon him: "Leave the sea still in its state of being parted, so that Allah may decree a matter that was to be done." Ar-rahw is also among the names of the crane bird, but it has no place in the interpretation of this verse. In my opinion it is more likely that it was named rahw for its stillness, and that it is always at leisure.

Then Allah, the Exalted, began to marvel at the abundance of the lofty, great matters they left behind in the world. "Kam" is a noun indicating multiplicity. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 44, verses 29–36:

Allah the Exalted said:

﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep for them, nor were they given respite.﴾ ﴿And We certainly rescued the Children of Israel from the humiliating torment,﴾ ﴿from Pharaoh. Indeed, he was haughty and one of the extravagant.﴾ ﴿And We chose them knowingly over the worlds.﴾ ﴿And We gave them of the signs that contained a manifest trial.﴾ ﴿Indeed, these [people] are saying:﴾ ﴿"It is only our first death, and we will not be resurrected.﴾ ﴿So bring our forefathers, if you should be truthful."﴾

(p. 578) This verse negates that the heaven and the earth wept over the people of Pharaoh. The wording therefore implies that the heaven and the earth have a weeping, and the interpreters (al-mutawwilun) differed about its meaning. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr, may Allah be pleased with them, said: when a believing man dies, the place of his worship weeps for him from the earth for forty mornings, and from the heaven the place where his deed ascends weeps for him. They said: among the people of Pharaoh there was no one in this state, and this is the meaning of the verse. Al-Suddi and 'Ata' said: the weeping of the heaven is the reddening of its edges. They said: the heaven turned red on the day al-Husayn ibn 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with them both, was killed, and that was a weeping for him. This is the meaning of the verse.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The good meaning of the verse is that it is a splendid and eloquent metaphor (isti'ara) which implies belittling their affair, and that nothing changed concerning their destruction. This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And though their plotting was such that the mountains would be moved by it﴾ [Ibrahim: 46], according to the reading of the one who reads "li-tazula" with a kasra on the lam and a fatha on the verb, and makes "in" a negation. A similar meaning is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Two goats do not butt heads in it," which implies belittling. But these expressions are according to what was said concerning it, namely the killing of the disbelieving woman who used to harm the Prophet ﷺ. The magnitude of the story of Pharaoh and his people brings with it the beauty of the description and the splendour of the expression in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep for them﴾. Of the same kind is that the saying of Jarir be reversed:

"When the news of al-Zubayr arrived, the walls of Medina humbled themselves, and the lofty mountains bowed down."

So it is said, in belittling: "So-and-so died, and the mountains did not bow down," and the like.

(p. 579) In a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ he said: "No believer dies in a foreign land where his weepers are absent, except that the heaven and the earth weep over him," then he recited this verse. He also said: "Indeed, they do not weep over a disbeliever." Of the magnification through the weeping of great created beings is the saying of Yazid ibn Mufarrigh:

"The wind weeps for its sorrow, and the lightning flashes in the cloud."

And the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"The sun rises, not eclipsed, and the stars of the night and the moon weep over you."

(p. 580) And "munzarin" means: delayed and given respite.

Then He mentioned His favour upon the Children of Israel in delivering them from Pharaoh and his people. "The humiliating torment" is the slaughtering of the sons and the subjugation to humiliating labours such as building and digging, and others. In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it is "min 'adhab al-muhin" with the definite article "al-" removed from "al-'adhab." His saying, the Exalted: ﴿from Pharaoh﴾ is a substitution (badal) for His saying: ﴿from the torment﴾. "Min" with a kasra on the mim is the reading of the majority, while Qatada narrated that Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, used to read it "man" with a fatha on the mim, "Fir'awnu" with a damma on the nun.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿knowingly﴾ means: according to something that preceded with Us concerning them and was established in Our knowledge, that it would be carried out. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿over the worlds﴾ intends: over all people. This is according to the interpretation mentioned earlier regarding knowledge, and the meaning is: We chose them for this deliverance and these blessings according to Our prior knowledge concerning them, and We singled them out for that over the rest of the world. It is also possible that His saying, the Exalted: ﴿knowingly﴾ means: with knowledge that is theirs, and virtues within them, and the meaning is: We chose them for prophethoods and messages. Then His saying, the Exalted: ﴿over the worlds﴾, in this interpretation, means: over the world of their time. The evidence for this is the superiority of the community of Muhammad ﷺ over them and their inferiority to it, and that the community of Muhammad ﷺ is "the best community brought forth for mankind." His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We gave them of the signs﴾ is a comprehensive expression for the miracles of Musa, peace be upon him, and the lessons that appeared among the people of Pharaoh, such as the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and other things, and for what Allah bestowed upon the Children of Israel, such as the shading cloud, the manna and the quails, and other things, for the word "signs" encompasses all of this. "Bala'" (trial) in this place means: testing and examination, and this is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya: 35]. And "mubin" here means: clear.

Then He mentioned the Quraysh and related their words, in the form of denouncing their saying when they denied what is permissible in reason. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, these [people] are saying:﴾ ﴿"It is only our first death"﴾, that is: the final end of our affair and the limit of our existence is only at our death. ﴿"And we will not be resurrected"﴾, that is: we will not be raised up. It is said: Allah "anshara" the dead, so he "nushira" (is raised). The saying of the Quraysh: ﴿"So bring our forefathers"﴾ is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, except that (p. 581) since the Prophet ﷺ, in his sayings and deeds, was ascribed to Allah the Exalted and through an angel, they addressed him as one addresses a group, while they meant him, his Lord, the Exalted, and His angels. In this verse the disbelievers requested that some of their forefathers be brought back to life for them, and they named Qusayy, so that they could ask them about what they had seen in the Hereafter. This verse does not fully refute them, since its explanation and its affirmation are found in other verses of the Book of Allah, the Exalted, for Allah, the Exalted, has affirmed the resurrection from the graves at an appointed term that no one can exceed. The examples of the dead earth and the condition of plants have already clarified the matter of resurrection from the graves.

"The sun rises, not eclipsed, and the stars of the night and the moon weep over you."

This verse does not fully refute them, since its explanation and its affirmation are found in other verses of the Book of Allah, the Exalted, for Allah, the Exalted, has affirmed the resurrection from the graves at an appointed term that no one can exceed. ﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep for them, nor were they given respite.﴾ ﴿And We certainly rescued the Children of Israel from the humiliating torment,﴾ ﴿from Pharaoh. Indeed, he was haughty and one of the extravagant.﴾ ﴿And We chose them knowingly over the worlds.﴾ ﴿And We gave them of the signs that contained a manifest trial.﴾ ﴿Indeed, these [people] are saying:﴾ ﴿"It is only our first death, and we will not be resurrected.﴾ ﴿So bring our forefathers, if you should be truthful."﴾

They said: among the people of Pharaoh there was no one in this state, and this is the meaning of the verse. Al-Suddi and 'Ata' said: the weeping of the heaven is the reddening of its edges. They said: the heaven turned red on the day al-Husayn ibn 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with them both, was killed, and that was a weeping for him. This is the meaning of the verse.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 44, verses 37–44:

His Exalted and Majestic words:

﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba' and those before them? We destroyed them, for they were criminals.﴾ ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ ﴿We did not create them except with truth, but most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is their appointed time, all of them.﴾ ﴿The Day when no master will avail his client in anything, nor will they be helped.﴾ ﴿Except for those on whom Allah has mercy. Indeed, He is the Almighty, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the tree of al-Zaqqum﴾ ﴿is the food of the sinful.﴾

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba' and those before them?﴾ This is a rhetorical question containing a warning. Tubba' was a king of the Himyar, and every one of their kings was called "Tubba'" (tubba', a title of the Himyarite kings). However, the one referred to in this verse is a righteous man from among the Tubba'a. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: Allah, Exalted is He, censured his people but did not censure him, and the scholars forbade reviling him. It was narrated from the Prophet ﷺ through the route of Sahl ibn Sa'd: "That this Tubba' embraced Islam and believed in Allah, Exalted is He." It is also narrated that this occurred at the hands of People of the Book who were in his presence. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: Tubba' was a prophet. Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "I do not know whether Tubba' was a prophet or not." Ibn Jubayr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: he is the one who clothed the Ka'bah. Ibn Ishaq mentioned him in the Sirah, and Allah knows best.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, they were criminals.﴾ He means: by disbelief. One group read "annahum" with a fath on the alif, while the majority read it with a kasrah.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth…﴾ This is a statement containing a reminder and a warning. His words ﴿except with truth﴾ mean: with that which is necessary, leading to good things and the overflowing of gifts. ﴿The Day of Decision﴾ is the Day of Resurrection, and this is the report of the Resurrection, a matter which reason allows and which the Shari'ah affirms through this verse and others. The word "mawla" in this verse encompasses all kinds of "mawali": kinship relations, mawali by manumission, and mawali by friendship. As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿nor will they be helped﴾: if the pronoun is taken to refer to all creation, then "min" in His words ﴿except for those on whom Allah has mercy﴾ may be in the accusative position as an exceptive of the connected type (istithna' muttasil). If the pronoun is taken to refer to the disbelievers, then the exception is disconnected (istithna' munqati'), and it may be in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), with the predicate omitted; its implied sense being: "for indeed some of them will avail others in intercession and the like," or its implied sense being: "for indeed Allah will help him."

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the tree of al-Zaqqum, is the food of the sinful﴾. It is narrated from Ibn Zayd that "al-athim" (the sinful) referred to here is Abu Jahl, but in meaning it encompasses every sinner, that is, every merchant who earns sin. It is narrated from Hammam that Abu al-Darda' taught a Bedouin, and he would say "ta'am al-yatim" (food of the orphan). Abu al-Darda' corrected him many times, but he did not learn it, so he said to him: say "ta'am al-fajir" (food of the wicked), and it was recited thus; and this is by way of explanation. It is the cursed tree mentioned in the Qur'an, growing at the root of Hell. It is narrated that when this verse was revealed, and people pointed it out to Abu Jahl, he gathered dates with butter, then invited people to it and said to them: "Eat zaqqum, for zaqqum is the dates of Yathrib with butter, and it is my food which Muhammad has spoken of."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He intended by this a kind of sophistry and deception upon the ignorant.

[p. 583]

The words of the Most High:

﴿Like molten brass, it boils in the bellies,﴾ ﴿like the boiling of scalding water.﴾ ﴿Seize him and drag him into the midst of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿Then pour over his head the torment of scalding water.﴾ ﴿Taste it! Indeed, you were the mighty, the noble.﴾ ﴿This is what you used to doubt.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in a secure station,﴾ ﴿among gardens and springs,﴾ ﴿clad in fine silk and brocade, facing one another.﴾ ﴿So it is; and We will pair them with wide-eyed maidens.﴾ ﴿There they will call for every kind of fruit, in security.﴾ ﴿They will not taste death there, except the first death; and He will protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿As a bounty from your Lord. That is the great triumph.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have made it easy in your tongue, so that they may be reminded.﴾ ﴿So wait; indeed, they are waiting.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them, said: "al-Muhl" is the sediment of olive oil and its dregs. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, also may Allah be pleased with them, said: "al-Mahl" is whatever melts of gold, silver, iron, lead, or the like. Al-Hasan said: Ibn Mas'ud was in charge of the treasury of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, in Kufa. One day he melted broken silver, and when it had liquefied, he said: "Let in whoever is at the door." They entered, and he said to them: "This is the most similar thing we have seen in this world to al-Muhl."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning is that this tree, when the disbeliever in Hell eats of it, becomes inside his belly and acts as hot al-Muhl acts, through burning and corruption. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr read "taghli" with a taa' (تَغْلِي), meaning: the tree. This is the reading of 'Amr ibn Maymun, Abu Razin, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Ibn Muhaysin, and Talha. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim in the transmission of Hafs read "yaghli" with a yaa' (يَغْلِي), referring to the food. This is the reading of Mujahid and al-Hasan, according to one report from him. "Al-Hamim" is the hot water that gives off vapour from its boiling.

As for the words of the Most High: ﴿Seize him and drag him﴾ and so on, the meaning is: on that Day it will be said to the angels concerning this sinner: "Seize him and drag him." "Al-'Utull" is driving with violence, humiliation, and strong, continuous pushing, as a perpetrator of crimes is always driven. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Ibn 'Amir read "fa'tilu-hu" with a ḍamma on the taa' (فاعْتِلُوهُ), and the rest read it with a kasra. The ḍamma has also been transmitted from Abu 'Amr, and both readings have been transmitted from al-Hasan, Qatada, and al-A'raj. "Al-Sawa'" means the middle; it has also been said to mean the most exalted, and these amount to the same thing, since the most exalted of such things is always in the middle. The verse implies that the disbeliever will have scalding water of Hell poured over his head, which is what boils in it from melted substances. This is like the words of the Most High: ﴿Scalding water will be poured over their heads﴾ [al-Hajj: 19]. Some rulers of Madina took this view, for he used to pour wine over the head of one who drank it, or was found with it, as a punishment and a discipline for him. Ibn Habib mentioned this in al-Wadiha.

The words of the Most High: ﴿Taste it! Indeed, you were the mighty, the noble﴾ are addressed in the sense of this rebuke. It is narrated from Qatada that when Abu Jahl said, after the revelation of: ﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum﴾ [al-Dukhan: 43] ﴿is the food of the sinner﴾ [al-Dukhan: 44]: "Does Muhammad threaten me, while I am between its two mountains, more mighty and more noble than him?" Then these verses were revealed, and at the end of them: ﴿Taste it! Indeed, you were the mighty, the noble﴾, meaning: according to your claim. This is like the words of Jarir:

"Did not the one whom marks were branded on... become a warning, O flower of Yemen?"

He says this to the poet who named himself by it, in his words:

"Convey to Kulayb, and convey from yourself to its poet, that I am the mighty, and that I am the flower of Yemen."

So Jarir's line was in response to this mockery. The majority read "innaka" with a kasra on the alif (إنَّكَ), while al-Kisa'i alone read "anna-ka" with a fatha on the alif (أنَّكَ). The meaning is the same in intent, though the grammatical derivation differs. Al-Husayn ibn 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with them both, recited it with a fatha on the alif from the pulpit; al-Kisa'i attributed it to him and followed him in it.

[p. 585]

The words of the Most High: ﴿Indeed, this is what you used to doubt﴾ are an expression of a statement that will be said to the disbelievers at their punishment, meaning: this is the Hereafter and Hell, which you used to doubt.

Then the Most High mentioned the state of the God-fearing immediately after the mention of the state of the disbeliever, to show the difference. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "fi muqamin amin" with a ḍamma on the mim (فِي مُقامٍ أمِينٍ). This is the reading of Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Qatada, 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, al-Hasan, and al-A'raj. The rest read "fi maqamin amin" with a fatha on the mim (فِي مَقامٍ أمِينٍ). This is the reading of Abu Raja', 'Isa, Yahya, and al-A'mash. "Amin" means that changes are secured in it, so it is like fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, meaning: safe in it. 'Asim read the ayn of "'uyun" with a kasra (عِيُونٍ). Abu Hatim said: this is rejected by the scholars, and similar to it are "shuyukh" and "buyut," with a kasra on the shin and the ba'. "Al-Sundus" is the fine silk, and "al-Istabraq" is its coarse kind. Ibn Muhaysin read "wa-istabraqin" with wasl and a fatha on the qaf (وَإسْتَبْرَقٍ). The words of the Most High: ﴿facing one another﴾ describe the gatherings of the people of Paradise, because none of them turns his back on another in the gatherings.

The words of the Most High: ﴿So it is; and We will pair them﴾ mean: the matter is so. The majority read "'in" (عِينٍ), which is the plural of 'aina' (wide-eyed). Ibn Mas'ud read "bi-'isin 'in" (بِعِيسٍ عِينٍ), which is the plural of 'aisa' (white), meaning the white ones, and so is the case with camels. 'Ikrima read "bi-hurin 'in" (بِحُورِ عِينٍ) without tanwin on "hur," and made it an idafa to "'in." Abu al-Fath said: the idafa here conveys what an adjective conveys. Abu Qurasafa related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Removing rubbish from the mosque is among the bridal gifts of the wide-eyed maidens."

The words of the Most High: ﴿There they will call﴾ mean: they will call for servants and attendants.

The words of the Most High: ﴿except the first death﴾: some scholars interpreted "illa" as "siwa" (except/other than), and al-Tabari considered this weak and interpreted it as "ba'du" (after). His weakening of it is not correct; rather, the meaning is sound and consistent with "siwa." As for the meaning of the verse, it clearly states that He negated for them the tasting of death, and that nothing will reach them of that beyond what has already occurred in this world.

The pronoun in the words of the Most High: ﴿We have made it easy﴾ refers to the Qur'an. The words ﴿in your tongue﴾ mean in the language of the Arabs; it does not mean the bodily organ. The words of the Most High: ﴿So wait; indeed, they are waiting﴾ mean: wait for Our help to you; indeed, they are waiting, according to their supposition, for the reversal of fortune against you. In this verse there is a promise to him (ﷺ) and a threat to them, and in it there is a permission to disengage, and this and what followed it is abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword.

The commentary on Surat al-Dukhan is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

'Ikrima read "bi-hurin 'in" (بِحُورِ عِينٍ) without tanwin on "hur," and made it an idafa to "'in." Abu al-Fath said: the idafa here conveys what an adjective conveys. Abu Qurasafa related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Removing rubbish from the mosque is among the bridal gifts of the wide-eyed maidens."

The words of the Most High: ﴿There they will call﴾ mean: they will call for servants and attendants.

The words of the Most High: ﴿except the first death﴾: some scholars interpreted "illa" as "siwa" (except/other than), and al-Tabari considered this weak and interpreted it as "ba'du" (after). His weakening of it is not correct; rather, the meaning is sound and consistent with "siwa." As for the meaning of the verse, it clearly states that He negated for them the tasting of death, and that nothing will reach them of that beyond what has already occurred in this world.

The pronoun in the words of the Most High: ﴿We have made it easy﴾ refers to the Qur'an. The words ﴿in your tongue﴾ mean in the language of the Arabs; it does not mean the bodily organ. The words of the Most High: ﴿So wait; indeed, they are waiting﴾ mean: wait for Our help to you; indeed, they are waiting, according to their supposition, for the reversal of fortune against you. In this verse there is a promise to him (ﷺ) and a threat to them, and in it there is a permission to disengage, and this and what followed it is abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword.

The commentary on Surat al-Dukhan is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

The words of the Most High:

﴿Like molten brass, it boils in the bellies,﴾ ﴿like the boiling of scalding water.﴾ ﴿Seize him and drag him into the midst of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿Then pour over his head the torment of scalding water.﴾ ﴿Taste it! Indeed, you were the mighty, the noble.﴾ ﴿This is what you used to doubt.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in a secure station,﴾ ﴿among gardens and springs,﴾ ﴿clad in fine silk and brocade, facing one another.﴾ ﴿So it is; and We will pair them with wide-eyed maidens.﴾ ﴿There they will call for every kind of fruit, in security.﴾ ﴿They will not taste death there, except the first death; and He will protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿As a bounty from your Lord. That is the great triumph.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have made it easy in your tongue, so that they may be reminded.﴾ ﴿So wait; indeed, they are waiting.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them, said: "al-Muhl" is the sediment of olive oil and its dregs. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, also may Allah be pleased with them, said: "al-Mahl" is whatever melts of gold, silver, iron, lead, or the like. Al-Hasan said: Ibn Mas'ud was in charge of the treasury of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, in Kufa. One day he melted broken silver, and when it had liquefied, he said: "Let in whoever is at the door." They entered, and he said to them: "This is the most similar thing we have seen in this world to al-Muhl."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning is that this tree, when the disbeliever in Hell eats of it, becomes inside his belly and acts as hot al-Muhl acts, through burning and corruption. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr read "taghli" with a taa' (تَغْلِي), meaning: the tree. This is the reading of 'Amr ibn Maymun, Abu Razin, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Ibn Muhaysin, and Talha. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim in the transmission of Hafs read "yaghli" with a yaa' (يَغْلِي), referring to the food. This is the reading of Mujahid and al-Hasan, according to one report from him. "Al-Hamim" is the hot water that gives off vapour from its boiling.

As for the words of the Most High: ﴿Seize him and drag him﴾ and so on, the meaning is: on that Day it will be said to the angels concerning this sinner: "Seize him and drag him." "Al-'Utull" is driving with violence, humiliation, and strong, continuous pushing, as a perpetrator of crimes is always driven. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Ibn 'Amir read "fa'tilu-hu" with a ḍamma on the taa' (فاعْتِلُوهُ), and the rest read it with a kasra. The ḍamma has also been transmitted from Abu 'Amr, and both readings have been transmitted from al-Hasan, Qatada, and al-A'raj. "Al-Sawa'" means the middle; it has also been said to mean the most exalted, and these amount to the same thing, since the most exalted of such things is always in the middle. The verse implies that the disbeliever will have scalding water of Hell poured over his head, which is what boils in it from melted substances. This is like the words of the Most High: ﴿Scalding water will be poured over their heads﴾ [al-Hajj: 19]. Some rulers of Madina took this view, for he used to pour wine over the head of one who drank it, or was found with it, as a punishment and a discipline for him. Ibn Habib mentioned this in al-Wadiha.

The words of the Most High: ﴿Taste it! Indeed, you were the mighty, the noble﴾ are addressed in the sense of this rebuke. It is narrated from Qatada that when Abu Jahl said, after the revelation of: ﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum﴾ [al-Dukhan: 43] ﴿is the food of the sinner﴾ [al-Dukhan: 44]: "Does Muhammad threaten me, while I am between its two mountains, more mighty and more noble than him?" Then these verses were revealed, and at the end of them: ﴿Taste it! Indeed, you were the mighty, the noble﴾, meaning: according to your claim. This is like the words of Jarir:

"Did not the one whom marks were branded on... become a warning, O flower of Yemen?"

He says this to the poet who named himself by it, in his words:

"Convey to Kulayb, and convey from yourself to its poet, that I am the mighty, and that I am the flower of Yemen."

So Jarir's line was in response to this mockery. The majority read "innaka" with a kasra on the alif (إنَّكَ), while al-Kisa'i alone read "anna-ka" with a fatha on the alif (أنَّكَ). The meaning is the same in intent, though the grammatical derivation differs. Al-Husayn ibn 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with them both, recited it with a fatha on the alif from the pulpit; al-Kisa'i attributed it to him and followed him in it.

The words of the Most High: ﴿Indeed, this is what you used to doubt﴾ are an expression of a statement that will be said to the disbelievers at their punishment, meaning: this is the Hereafter and Hell, which you used to doubt.

Then the Most High mentioned the state of the God-fearing immediately after the mention of the state of the disbeliever, to show the difference. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "fi muqamin amin" with a ḍamma on the mim (فِي مُقامٍ أمِينٍ). This is the reading of Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Qatada, 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, al-Hasan, and al-A'raj. The rest read "fi maqamin amin" with a fatha on the mim (فِي مَقامٍ أمِينٍ). This is the reading of Abu Raja', 'Isa, Yahya, and al-A'mash. "Amin" means that changes are secured in it, so it is like fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, meaning: safe in it. 'Asim read the ayn of "'uyun" with a kasra (عِيُونٍ). Abu Hatim said: this is rejected by the scholars, and similar to it are "shuyukh" and "buyut," with a kasra on the shin and the ba'. "Al-Sundus" is the fine silk, and "al-Istabraq" is its coarse kind. Ibn Muhaysin read "wa-istabraqin" with wasl and a fatha on the qaf (وَإسْتَبْرَقٍ). The words of the Most High: ﴿facing one another﴾ describe the gatherings of the people of Paradise, because none of them turns his back on another in the gatherings.
